lessons.title: Lehman Brothers and the Week the System Froze

body.text: Lehman Brothers did not collapse simply because it lost money. It collapsed because, almost overnight, nobody would lend to it. For a heavily leveraged firm, trust is the only thing standing between business as usual and bankruptcy.

children.text: In the last lesson you saw how subprime loans were packaged and spread through the financial system. This lesson covers the moment the bomb went off. In September 2008, a 158 year old investment bank failed, the world's largest insurer needed an emergency government loan, a "safe" money market fund lost investors' money, and banks everywhere stopped lending to each other. Within two weeks, the panic reached a queue of worried depositors outside ICICI Bank branches in India.
March 2008: The Warning From Bear Stearns

markDefs.definition: The repurchase agreement market, where financial firms borrow cash, often overnight, by pledging securities as collateral and agreeing to buy them back later. If lenders refuse to roll over these loans, a firm can run out of cash within days.

children.text: Bear Stearns, the fifth largest US investment bank, had loaded up on mortgage securities and funded itself with enormous amounts of short-term borrowing. Much of that borrowing came through the
repo market
, where firms borrow cash overnight against securities as collateral. In March 2008, lenders and clients lost confidence and pulled their money. Bear Stearns ran out of cash in days.

body.label: Bear Stearns, 16 March 2008
body.context: JPMorgan Chase agreed to buy Bear Stearns for about $2 a share, with the New York Fed covering up to $29 billion of Bear's riskier assets. After fury from shareholders, the price was raised to about $10 a share on 24 March, still a fraction of its value a year earlier.

children.text: The rescue calmed markets for a few months, and many took the wrong lesson from it: that the US authorities would never let a big investment bank fail. Six months later, that assumption was tested.

columns.label: A Traditional Bank Run
points: Ordinary depositors fear the bank will fail
They queue at branches and ATMs to withdraw cash
Visible and slow: it takes days of queues to drain a bank
In India, DICGC deposit insurance of up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank reduces the incentive to panic

columns.label: A Wholesale Funding Run
points: Professional lenders fear a firm will fail
They refuse to roll over overnight repo loans or demand far more collateral
Invisible and fast: billions can leave in a single day
No deposit insurance protects these lenders, so they run first and ask questions later
Examples: Bear Stearns in March 2008, Lehman Brothers in September 2008

body.title: How Does a $639 Billion Firm Fail in Days?
body.question: Lehman Brothers reported $639 billion of assets when it filed for bankruptcy. What best explains how a firm that size could collapse within days?
options: All $639 billion of its assets became worthless overnight
It depended on short-term borrowing, and once lenders stopped rolling over its loans it could not raise cash fast enough by selling assets
US law required it to close once its share price fell below $10
Its employees withdrew their salaries all at once
body.explanation: Lehman financed long-term, hard to sell assets such as mortgage securities with borrowing that had to be renewed daily. With leverage of about 31 to 1, even modest losses raised doubts about its solvency. Once lenders and trading partners pulled back, Lehman needed cash immediately, but its assets could only be sold slowly, and in a panic, at huge discounts. A funding run can kill a firm long before its losses are fully counted.

children.text: The Week the System Froze

events.title: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac Taken Over
events.description: The US government places the two giant mortgage finance companies into conservatorship, effectively nationalising them.

events.title: The Lost Weekend
events.description: Officials and bankers search for a buyer for Lehman. Talks with Bank of America and Barclays fail, and the US government refuses to put public money behind a deal.

events.title: Lehman Files for Bankruptcy
events.description: Lehman Brothers files with $639 billion of assets, the largest bankruptcy in US history. The same day, Bank of America agrees to buy Merrill Lynch for $50 billion. The Dow falls 504.48 points, and in Mumbai the Sensex falls 469.54 points, or about 3.35%, to 13,531.27.

events.title: AIG Rescued, a Money Fund Breaks
events.description: The Federal Reserve lends up to $85 billion to AIG, the insurance giant, in exchange for a 79.9% stake. That afternoon, the Reserve Primary Fund announces its shares are worth 97 cents, not $1, after writing its $785 million of Lehman debt down to zero.

events.title: The End of Wall Street as It Was
events.description: Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the last two big independent investment banks, convert into bank holding companies regulated by the Federal Reserve, gaining access to emergency central bank funding.

events.title: The Largest Bank Failure in US History
events.description: Regulators seize Washington Mutual, with $307 billion of assets, and sell its banking operations to JPMorgan Chase.

events.title: Congress Says No
events.description: The US House of Representatives rejects a $700 billion bank rescue plan. The Dow falls 777.68 points, or 6.98%, then its largest ever one day points fall.

events.title: Panic Reaches India
events.description: False rumours about ICICI Bank's exposure to Lehman spread by SMS, and depositors queue at some branches and ATMs to withdraw cash.

events.title: TARP Becomes Law
events.description: A revised $700 billion Troubled Asset Relief Program is signed into law, allowing the US Treasury to inject capital into banks.

children.text: Why Lehman's Failure Spread So Far: Counterparty Risk

markDefs.definition: The risk that the other party to a financial contract, such as a borrower, trading partner or insurer, fails to meet its obligations.

children.text: Lehman was not an island. It had borrowed from money market funds, traded derivatives with hundreds of banks, and held clients' assets around the world. Every one of those relationships carried
counterparty risk
. When Lehman failed, nobody knew exactly who was owed what, or who else might be next. So everyone assumed the worst about everyone else.

markDefs.definition: Contracts that work like insurance against a borrower defaulting. The buyer pays regular premiums, and the seller pays out if the borrower or security defaults.

children.text: AIG shows how hidden these links were. The insurer had sold huge amounts of
credit default swaps

promising to cover losses on mortgage securities. As those securities fell, AIG owed billions in collateral it did not have. Its failure would have blown holes in the balance sheets of banks across the world, which is why the Fed rescued AIG a day after letting Lehman go.
Here is how Lehman's failure reached ordinary companies within 48 hours:
Lehman files for bankruptcy, and the short-term debt it issued becomes nearly worthless.
The Reserve Primary Fund, a money market fund that held $785 million of that debt, breaks the buck.
Investors who believed money market funds were as safe as cash rush to withdraw from funds across the industry. Redemption requests at the Reserve Primary Fund alone pass $40 billion in two days.
To meet withdrawals, money market funds stop buying commercial paper, the short-term IOUs that big companies issue.
Companies that relied on commercial paper to pay suppliers and salaries suddenly struggle to borrow at all.

body.label: Reserve Primary Fund, 16 September 2008
body.context: A 3% loss sounds small. But money market funds were sold as near cash that should never fall below $1. Breaking that promise told investors that nothing was safe, which is what turned a fund problem into a system wide run.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The risk that the other party to a financial contract fails to pay what it owes is called ___ risk.
body.explanation: Counterparty risk is what turned Lehman's failure into a global freeze. Banks could not see each other's exposures, so they treated every counterparty as a possible Lehman and stopped lending.

children.text: Measuring Fear: The LIBOR-OIS Spread

markDefs.definition: The gap between the rate banks charged each other for unsecured three month loans (LIBOR) and a near risk-free rate linked to expected central bank policy (OIS). A wider spread means banks fear lending to each other.

children.text: How do you measure trust between banks? One of the best gauges is the
LIBOR-OIS spread

. In normal times, a bank lending to another bank for three months charged only slightly more than the near risk-free rate. When banks fear each other might fail, they demand much more, or refuse to lend at all.

body.title: The Price of Distrust: Three Month LIBOR-OIS Spread (approximate, basis points)

children.text: A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 365 basis points is 3.65 percentage points. Before the crisis, the spread moved within a narrow band of about 7 to 20 basis points. After Lehman, it shot to around 365.

body.title: Your Turn: The Cost of Distrust
body.prompt: A bank needs to borrow $100 million for three months. In normal times it pays 0.20 percentage points (20 basis points) above the risk-free rate. On 10 October 2008 it would have paid 3.65 percentage points (365 basis points) above. How much extra interest, in US dollars, does the crisis spread cost for those three months?
body.explanation: Extra spread = 3.65% minus 0.20% = 3.45 percentage points a year. For three months: $100 million × 3.45% × 3 ÷ 12 = about $862,500. And that assumes another bank would lend at all. In October 2008, many simply refused, whatever the price.

children.text: The Rescue: From "Let It Fail" to "Whatever It Takes"

body.caption: How the Biggest Institutions Fared in 2008

cells: Sold to JPMorgan Chase for about $10 a share, with Fed support
Taken over by the US government, 7 September
Heavy mortgage losses, expected to be next
Sold to Bank of America for $50 billion
Could not meet collateral calls on credit default swaps
Rescued with an $85 billion Fed loan for a 79.9% stake
Became Fed-regulated bank holding companies, 21 September
Seized and sold to JPMorgan Chase, 25 September
$700 billion TARP signed 3 October; Fed cuts rates to 0% to 0.25% on 16 December

body.text: Notice the pattern. Bear Stearns was rescued, Lehman was not, and AIG was rescued the very next day. That inconsistency made the panic worse, because investors could no longer predict which firms the government would save. Uncertainty about the rules can be as damaging as the losses themselves.

body.title: Should Lehman Have Been Saved? The Moral Hazard Debate

markDefs.definition: The risk that people or firms take bigger risks when they expect someone else to bear the cost if things go wrong, for example if they expect a government bailout.

children.text: The decision to let Lehman fail is still debated. At its heart is the idea of
moral hazard
The case for letting it fail:

rescuing every big firm teaches bankers that profits are private and losses are public, encouraging even more reckless risk taking next time. After Bear Stearns, officials worried that another rescue would make that problem worse.
The case that it should have been saved:
the cost of Lehman's disorderly collapse, frozen credit markets, a global recession and far larger rescues afterwards, was much greater than the cost of a rescue would have been.
The official explanation:
US officials later argued they lacked the legal authority to lend to Lehman, because it did not have enough good collateral to secure a loan. Some economists dispute this.

India's regulators face the same dilemma. When Yes Bank ran into trouble in 2020, RBI and the government arranged a rescue led by SBI rather than letting it fail, to protect depositors and confidence in the banking system.
Within Two Weeks, the Panic Reached India

On the day Lehman failed, the Sensex fell 3.35%. Lehman's own Indian footprint was large: its Powai offices in Mumbai employed about 3,000 people, including about 1,200 IT professionals, in back office and technology roles. Weeks later, Japan's Nomura agreed to buy these operations, and most of the jobs survived.

The more frightening moment came on 30 September 2008. SMS messages spread claiming that ICICI Bank, India's largest private sector bank, was about to collapse because of its Lehman exposure. In reality, its UK subsidiary had about $80 million of exposure to Lehman, small relative to the bank's size. Still, depositors queued at some branches and ATMs. The bank called the rumours "baseless and malicious". In an unusual step, RBI issued a public statement that ICICI Bank had adequate liquidity and that RBI would provide cash if needed. Finance Minister P. Chidambaram pushed the bank's leadership to reassure the public on television. The run stopped. Lesson 3.3 picks up the full story of how 2008 hit India.

body.title: The Forwarded Message About Your Bank
body.scenario: You wake up to a WhatsApp forward in three family groups: "URGENT: [Your bank] has huge losses from a foreign bank collapse. Withdraw your money TODAY before it is frozen." You have ₹3.5 lakh in a savings account and a ₹4 lakh fixed deposit at that bank. Your parents are already heading to the branch.
body.prompt: Using the ICICI Bank episode and what you know about deposit insurance, what should you do, and what would you check before acting?
body.modelAnswer: Start by not joining the run, because runs are self-fulfilling: if enough people withdraw at once, even a healthy bank can struggle for cash. Next, check the facts from official sources rather than forwards: the bank's own statements and stock exchange filings on NSE and BSE, any statement from RBI, and reports from established financial news outlets. In 2008, the ICICI Bank rumours were false, and RBI publicly stated that the bank had adequate liquidity. Then check your actual risk. DICGC insures deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, covering principal and interest across savings and fixed deposits combined. Your total of ₹7.5 lakh exceeds that limit by ₹2.5 lakh, so that portion is not insured. That is a reason to plan calmly, not to panic: when the fixed deposit matures, or if you choose to break it after weighing any penalty, you could move the excess to a different bank so that your deposits in each bank stay within the insured limit. Finally, recall how Indian regulators have handled troubled banks. In cases like Yes Bank in 2020, RBI and the government arranged rescues that protected depositors. Speak to your parents with facts, and treat urgent forwarded warnings with scepticism.

body.title: How Safe Are Your Bank Deposits?
steps: List every bank where you hold savings accounts, current accounts or fixed deposits, including joint accounts
Add up principal plus interest held in each individual bank
Check whether any single bank holds more than the DICGC insured limit of ₹5 lakh for you
Look up the DICGC website to confirm your bank is an insured bank and to understand how the cover works
Find your bank's latest capital adequacy ratio and gross NPA ratio in its quarterly results on its investor relations page
If you hold more than ₹5 lakh in one bank, consider spreading deposits across banks as they mature
Save the official RBI and bank websites, so you check facts there first the next time a rumour appears

body.label: DICGC: Deposit Insurance in India
body.description: The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, a wholly owned subsidiary of RBI, explains how deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank are insured and lists insured banks.

cards.definition: Where financial firms borrow cash, often overnight, against securities as collateral. A loss of confidence can shut a firm out within days.
When professional lenders refuse to renew short-term loans to a financial firm, draining its cash far faster than a depositor run.
The risk that the other party to a financial contract fails to meet its obligations.
An insurance-like contract that pays out if a borrower or security defaults. AIG sold huge amounts on mortgage securities.
When a money market fund's share value falls below $1, as the Reserve Primary Fund's did on 16 September 2008.
A gauge of fear between banks. It jumped from about 7 to 20 basis points before the crisis to around 365 in October 2008.
The risk that firms take more risk when they expect someone else, such as the government, to cover their losses.
The US Troubled Asset Relief Program, a $700 billion rescue fund signed into law on 3 October 2008.

points: Leveraged firms that depend on short-term borrowing can fail within days once lenders lose trust, as Bear Stearns showed in March and Lehman in September 2008
Lehman's bankruptcy on 15 September 2008, with $639 billion of assets, was the largest in US history
Counterparty risk spread the damage: AIG needed an $85 billion rescue, and the Reserve Primary Fund broke the buck on its Lehman holdings
Fear between banks is measurable: the LIBOR-OIS spread jumped from under 20 basis points before the crisis to around 365 in October 2008
Inconsistent rescue decisions deepened the panic, until TARP and near zero interest rates signalled that authorities would do whatever it took
The panic reached India within days: the Sensex fell 3.35% on 15 September, and false rumours triggered a brief run on ICICI Bank before RBI's statement calmed depositors
